claim: A revolved solid-of-revolution mesh whose profile pinches to a near-zero radius at BOTH ends (e.g. via an authored (radius, z) profile like this project's revolve_closed_profile) creates an implicit long, thin, near-degenerate quad strip connecting the two near-axis tip rings end to end -- not a normal short pole. Under a Subdivision Surface modifier this produces a visible concave dimple/crater at the flat-cap end, not a clean rounded tip, because Catmull-Clark subdivision propagates curvature poorly across that extreme-aspect-ratio connecting strip.
supporting_evidence: Directly observed and root-caused live on a held-out flashlight build (runs/2026-08-17_flashlight-model/): a beauty render (beauty_iso.png) of the front cap showed a clear concave crater, invisible in a flat black silhouette render of the same mesh. Diagnosed by querying the mesh directly: exactly 32 faces (one per radial segment) had all four vertices within 0.5 units of the revolution axis -- these connected the z=0 tail-tip ring directly to the z=25.4 front-tip ring, spanning the object's full length at near-zero radius. Confirmed by reading Ian McGlasham's 'A better cylinder' (pWOh9cWwYqU, 0:08-1:16): a naive n-gon or triangle-fan cylinder cap, once Subsurf is applied, is explicitly shown producing a visibly broken/pinched result ('that's a mess, it's nothing like a cylinder').
rejected_alternative: Assuming a flat-disc-to-near-zero-point profile segment is a safe way to close a revolved SubD-ready cap, and treating the resulting shading defect as a rendering/lighting artifact rather than a topology problem -- the defect was completely invisible in a silhouette-only check and only became apparent once a real shaded beauty render was produced.
reason: This is a concrete, previously-unknown limitation of this project's own revolve_closed_profile helper when used for SubD-ready primary forms: it is safe for the geometry itself (0 non-manifold, 0 degenerate faces reported by mesh-health checks) but not safe for subsequent Subdivision Surface smoothing. Mesh-validity checks do not catch this -- only an actual shaded render does, which is why this project's silhouette-only comparisons had missed it.

transfer_tests.evidence: runs/2026-08-17_flashlight-model/stage_04_report.json and beauty_iso_v2.png/beauty_side_v2.png -- deleting the 32 identified near-axis 'spine' faces and re-capping each resulting open ring with a single ngon (fill_selection) via a typed decision transaction, then re-applying the same Subsurf + smooth-by-angle setup, produced a clean rounded cap with no dimpling. Mesh health after the fix: 480 verts, 928 edges, 450 faces, 0 non-manifold, 0 degenerate, 2 ngons (the two new tip caps, expected).

claim: The correct way to build a SubD-ready cylindrical/revolved primary form's end cap is: start from (or reduce to) a single n-gon or a small ring boundary at each tip, inset it (creating a proper 4-spoked-pole corner ring rather than a high-valence pole sitting directly on an edge), and either leave the innermost face as a single n-gon cap or (for a cleaner result) delete it and use a true Grid Fill to convert the circular boundary into a regular quad grid -- never leave a triangle fan or a long thin near-axis connecting strip as the cap.
supporting_evidence: Per the transcript, 1:14-4:34: starting from an n-gon-capped cylinder, insetting the cap face (~10%) moves the boundary loop away from the sharp top/bottom edge so corners read as 4-spoked poles instead of 3-spoked; a second, larger inset (~50%) creates room for a control loop; the remaining inner n-gon is deleted and the boundary is filled with Grid Fill (a true quad grid, not a pole); a matching control loop is added around the cross-section (via an inset on a selected ring of side faces) so curvature is held at both the cap boundary and the shoulder. The video's closing framing: 'we've really thought about the idea of an object having a top, a bottom, a cross section, and areas of curvature connecting these things.'
rejected_alternative: Leaving Blender's default cylinder primitive's own cap fill options (ngon with no further topology work, or triangle fan) as the final SubD-ready cap -- the video demonstrates both failing visibly under Subsurf, and this project's own flashlight build hit the same class of failure independently before this source was consulted.
reason: This project used the simpler half of this technique (delete the bad connector, cap with one n-gon each) to fix the flashlight's dimpling defect, and it worked -- but the FULL technique (control loops at every curvature transition, Grid Fill instead of a bare n-gon) was not yet applied and is the natural next refinement for this and future revolved SubD forms, especially at the neck/shoulder transition which currently has no explicit holding loop.
